Reinforcement learning: the problems behind the methods

From playing Breaking Bellman to the problems behind reinforcement learning: delayed credit, exploration, scale and learning from guesses.

October 20, 20265 min read

reinforcement-learningmachine-learning

Reinforcement learning

Part 0 of 5

  1. Reinforcement learning: the problems behind the methods
  2. RL methods: a family tree and a Q table
  3. Bootstrapping: learn before the reward arrives
  4. Function approximation: share a value, share an error
  5. On-policy and off-policy: whose future are we learning?
  6. The deadly triad: how a guess can train itself upward
Next: RL methods: a family tree and a Q table →

The deadly triad is what got me exploring reinforcement learning. Playing Breaking Bellman taught me about RL, and this series is where I’m sharing what I learn.

The triad brings together three useful ideas: learn before the outcome is known, share learning across situations, and reuse data collected by another policy. Together, they can create a feedback loop in which an error feeds the next prediction. To understand why, we first need the problems those ideas solve.

Part 0. Next: the method tree and a Q table.

In reinforcement learning, an agent takes actions, observes what happens and receives rewards. A policy is its rule for choosing actions. The aim is to earn more reward over time. The hard part is learning which choices will do that.

The reward arrives late

You win a game after a hundred moves. The final reward says the game went well, but which moves made it happen? The last move might have been obvious; an earlier choice may have opened the winning route.

This is credit assignment: connecting an outcome to the decisions that contributed to it. A robot reaching an object faces the same problem. It needs to learn about the approach and the grasp, even if success is only clear at the end.

We will use estimates of future reward to carry that information back to earlier choices. Part 1 makes those estimates visible in a table.

A good first result can hide a better choice

Imagine ten slot machines with unknown average payouts. One pays well on your first try. Should you keep pulling it, or spend some turns finding out about the others?

Repeating the best-looking choice is exploitation. Trying a less familiar one is exploration. Rewards can be noisy, so a lucky first result can keep you repeating a mediocre choice. Exploring costs something now, but it can improve later decisions.

Part 1’s bandit example compares those choices, then adds states and a longer future.

Waiting for the outcome can be expensive

We could finish each game before learning from it. But a long episode means a long wait, and one outcome can reflect many chance events.

Bootstrapping learns sooner by combining a reward we observed with an estimate of what comes next. That lets information travel before the final result arrives. It also means an inaccurate estimate can become part of the next lesson. Part 2 compares waiting, guessing and looking several steps ahead.

There are too many situations to learn separately

A small grid has a manageable number of cells. A camera image or a robot’s joint positions can describe far more situations than we can visit one by one. Learning a separate answer for each would leave almost everything unknown.

Function approximation shares learning through a model, such as a neural network. A lesson from one situation can improve a prediction elsewhere. It can also change a prediction that was already good. Part 3 follows both effects through one shared weight.

The data may come from different choices

A robot’s stored experience might come from an older controller. A learning agent might take random exploratory actions while trying to work out how a more decisive policy would behave.

The policy that supplies the data and the policy we want to evaluate can differ. Learning about the latter from the former is off-policy learning; on-policy learning evaluates the policy producing the experience. Reusing data is valuable, but the data must tell us enough about the choices we want to judge. An action never tried can remain unknown. Part 4 makes that difference concrete at the edge of a cliff.

A prediction can feed its own error

Now put those three ideas together. Bootstrapping uses a prediction in the target we learn toward. Function approximation lets one update change several predictions. Off-policy data can leave some of those predictions poorly corrected. The next target can then inherit an error that the previous update enlarged.

This combination is the deadly triad. It can make learning unstable; it does not make every such learner fail. Part 5 builds the feedback loop with two states and one weight, then examines ways to interrupt it.

The route through the series

  1. The method tree and a Q table: connect methods to their problems, then watch one table learn.
  2. Bootstrapping: choose how much observed reward to use before a guess. This also leads to Generalized Advantage Estimation (GAE), which mixes return lengths to assign action credit.
  3. Function approximation: see what changes when predictions share weights.
  4. On-policy and off-policy learning: separate the policy collecting data from the one being evaluated.
  5. The deadly triad: bring the three mechanisms together and examine stability.

The questions come first. Next, we will look at the tools people built to answer them.

Sources

The progression draws on Sutton and Barto, Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction, second edition: exploration in Chapter 2, returns and policies in Chapter 3, temporal-difference learning in Chapter 6, approximation in Chapter 9 and the deadly triad in Section 11.3. Van Hasselt and colleagues examine the interaction between the triad’s ingredients. The small slot-machine drawing shows how two initial payouts can mislead a greedy choice; the measured comparisons and their settings are in Part 1.
